title: How Intelligent Document Processing Is Changing Government Intake
summary: Intelligent document processing can dramatically reduce manual review time for government agencies. But extracting data from documents is not the same as verifying it. The trust problem requires a different solution.
body_markdown:
Intelligent document processing (IDP) has become one of the most discussed technologies in government digital services, and for good reason. Agencies that once employed staff to manually key data from scanned tax forms, benefits applications, and permit submissions are now automating that extraction. Processing times that once ran days or weeks can compress to minutes. The efficiency argument is real, and it has driven substantial adoption across federal and state programs.


But the efficiency argument covers only part of the problem. Extracting data from a document and confirming that the data is authentic are two different operations, and IDP handles the first while leaving the second largely unresolved. For agencies building intake infrastructure, this distinction shapes what technology can and cannot accomplish on its own.


## What IDP actually does


Intelligent document processing is the combination of optical character recognition (OCR), natural language processing (NLP), and machine learning (ML) classification applied to unstructured documents. OCR converts scanned images and PDFs into machine-readable text. NLP identifies what that text represents: names, dates, dollar amounts, addresses, identification numbers. ML classification routes the extracted data into the right fields of a structured record, often trained on labeled examples of the document types an agency regularly receives.


A mature IDP system can handle a wide range of document formats without requiring that each form be templated in advance. It can tolerate variations in layout, hand-printed characters, and degraded scan quality at accuracy rates that would have required human review just a few years ago. For high-volume programs (licensing agencies processing thousands of renewal applications per month, benefits programs receiving supporting documentation from applicants across a state) this matters operationally.


The output of an IDP pipeline is structured data: fields with values, confidence scores, and flags for human review when the system falls below a confidence threshold. What it is not is a statement about the trustworthiness of those values.


## Government use cases where IDP applies


The use cases are broad enough that almost any agency handling resident-submitted documentation has some application for IDP.


Benefits programs are among the clearest examples. A Medicaid or SNAP application typically requires income documentation, proof of residency, and identity documents. Most of that evidence arrives as uploaded photos, PDFs generated from third-party portals, or scans of paper documents. IDP can pull the relevant values out of those files automatically rather than relying on a caseworker to type them into a case management system.


Occupational licensing presents a similar pattern. An applicant submitting proof of education, prior licenses from other jurisdictions, or completion of a supervised practice period generates documentation that varies by source and format. IDP can normalize that variation into fields a licensing system can evaluate consistently.


Permit and inspection workflows involve large volumes of documentation from contractors, architects, and property owners, often submitted in batches and in non-standardized formats. IDP reduces the data-entry burden on agency staff and accelerates the workflow from submission to review.


In each of these contexts, the efficiency gain is genuine. Caseworkers spend less time typing and more time reviewing decisions. Processing backlogs shrink. Applications move faster through the queue.


## Extraction is not verification


Here is where the IDP story often stops when it should continue.


A document that has been processed by an IDP pipeline has had its content extracted. The agency now holds a structured record containing, for example, an applicant's name, employer, stated income, and employment dates. What the IDP system does not know, and cannot determine from the document alone, is whether that information is accurate.


Consider what an agency is actually relying on when it receives an uploaded pay stub or bank statement. The document was created by the applicant or someone on their behalf. It was submitted digitally, meaning it could have been modified before upload. Even if the document is visually authentic, the IDP system reads what is in the document, not what is actually true about the applicant's financial situation. A sophisticated forgery produces a confident extraction result.


This is not a new problem. Paper documents carried the same vulnerability. What has changed is that IDP, by making extraction faster and more automated, can create an operational rhythm in which documents flow through the intake pipeline without triggering the scrutiny that slower manual review used to force. Efficiency and oversight can move in opposite directions if the process is not designed carefully.


[Document intake infrastructure](https://blog.spruceid.com/documentintake-what-is-document-intake-the-foundation-of-government-digital-services/) , properly understood, involves more than moving documents from applicants to agency systems. It involves moving trustworthy data, and that requires the underlying evidence to carry some form of verifiable provenance, not just readable content.


## Why accuracy rates do not close the gap


IDP vendors often lead with accuracy metrics. A system that extracts data from documents with 98 or 99 percent accuracy is genuinely useful, but that accuracy applies to the extraction task (turning pixels into fields), not to the authenticity of the underlying content.


An agency that uses IDP to process income documentation is asking: "What does this document say the applicant earns?" A well-functioning IDP system answers that question reliably. The more important question is often: "Is this an accurate record, issued by an employer that actually employed this person?" IDP answers neither that question nor the question of whether the employer's system generated the record in the first place.


This matters for fraud exposure.[Document intake is a well-documented fraud vector](https://blog.spruceid.com/why-document-intake-is-a-fraud-vector-and-how-modern-systems-can-close-it/) in government programs, and automation does not reduce that exposure by itself. If anything, it can scale throughput in ways that allow fraudulent applications to move through the pipeline before review flags them.


The[case for automating document intake in benefits programs](https://blog.spruceid.com/documentintake-how-document-intake-automation-can-reduce-fraud-in-government-benefits-programs/) depends on pairing extraction efficiency with better mechanisms for confirming that extracted data reflects reality. Without that pairing, agencies are automating a step in a process that was already inadequately secured.


## What structured, verifiable data changes


The alternative to a document-centric intake model is an intake model that accepts data rather than documents, specifically data that carries cryptographic evidence of its source.


[Verifiable digital credentials](https://www.w3.org/TR/vc-data-model-2.0/?ref=blog.spruceid.com) issued by authoritative sources give agencies a way to receive income data, identity information, employment records, and professional licenses as structured data signed by the institution that holds the original record. The employer payroll system, the state licensing board, the federal wage-reporting infrastructure: each of these is capable of issuing a credential that an agency system can verify cryptographically without calling back to the source at the time of review.


When an applicant presents a verifiable digital credential rather than an uploaded document, the receiving agency can confirm three things: the credential was issued by a specific institution, the content has not been modified since issuance, and the credential is being presented by the person it was issued to. None of those assurances is available from an IDP-processed upload.[Verifiable digital credentials](https://blog.spruceid.com/digitalidentity-how-do-verifiable-digital-credentials-work-a-non-technical-explanation/) accomplish this through public-key cryptography, binding the issuer's signing key to the credential content in a way that any verifying party can confirm without a centralized lookup.


This is not a rejection of IDP. For agencies dealing with legacy document types that will not be replaced by structured credentials anytime soon, IDP remains a practical tool for reducing manual work. The point is that IDP and verifiable digital credentials address different parts of the intake problem, and treating one as a substitute for the other leaves a meaningful gap.


## IDP and structured credentials as complementary layers


A realistic modernization path for most agencies involves both approaches operating in parallel, with the mix shifting over time.


For document types where authoritative digital issuance exists (state-issued ID credentials, professional licenses, employment records from large employers with integrated payroll systems), agencies can accept verifiable digital credentials directly and skip the extraction problem entirely. The data arrives structured, authenticated, and ready for programmatic evaluation.


For document types where no authoritative digital issuance exists yet, IDP remains useful. A handwritten letter, a lease agreement, a utility bill, a document from a foreign institution: none of these will exist as a verifiable digital credential in the near term. IDP reduces the cost of processing them. But the agency should treat this data as unverified input that may require additional confirmation steps, not as authenticated evidence equivalent to a cryptographically signed record.


[Intake systems that fail to distinguish between authenticated and unauthenticated data](https://blog.spruceid.com/documentintake-5-signs-your-document-intake-system-is-creating-security-risks/) tend to make risk decisions uniformly across both, which means either over-relying on unverified uploads or under-utilizing the assurance that verifiable digital credentials provide.


The design principle worth applying is proportionality: the assurance level of the evidence should match the risk level of the decision. High-stakes eligibility determinations warrant stronger evidence than routine correspondence. IDP can serve the lower end of that spectrum. Verifiable digital credentials belong at the higher end, where the cost of relying on fabricated documentation is greatest.


## What the resident experience looks like in practice


One objection that comes up in program design conversations is whether residents can realistically be expected to present verifiable digital credentials rather than documents. The short answer is that the experience is simpler from the resident's side, not more complex.


Under a document-centric model, a resident applying for benefits must locate a document (a pay stub, a bank statement, a prior tax return), then photograph or scan it, then upload it, then wait for a caseworker to review it. If the document is illegible, incomplete, or in an unexpected format, the application stalls.


Under a credential-based model, the resident authorizes the release of specific data from an institution that holds the record. They do not need to find a document. They do not need to scan it. They present a credential from their wallet, and the receiving system receives structured, authenticated data.[The resident experience of submitting a verifiable digital credential](https://blog.spruceid.com/documentintake-what-does-a-resident-experience-when-they-submit-a-verifiable-digital-credential/) is generally faster and involves fewer points of failure than document upload.


The bottleneck in this model is credential issuance, not credential presentation. Agencies that want to accept verifiable digital credentials need the institutions generating the underlying data (employers, other government agencies, licensing boards) to issue credentials in standardized formats. That infrastructure is developing, but it is not yet universal. A realistic implementation plan addresses this by identifying which data sources are ready for credential-based exchange and which still require document-based handling.


## The intake problem is a trust problem


When agencies invest in IDP, they are solving a throughput problem. That is a legitimate operational concern. But the deeper challenge in document intake is a trust problem: how does an agency know that the data it receives accurately reflects the real-world situation of the applicant?


Faster extraction does not answer that question.[The transition from paper to structured data in government digital services](https://blog.spruceid.com/from-paper-to-structured-data-the-missing-link-in-government-digital-services/) requires attention to how that structure is produced, not only to whether it can be read efficiently. Data that arrives already structured and cryptographically signed by its source is categorically different from data that was extracted from a file the applicant uploaded.


IDP is a useful capability, and agencies that deploy it well will reduce manual labor and accelerate routine processing. But the agencies that will build the most resilient intake infrastructure are the ones that treat IDP as one layer in a broader system, one that eventually gives way, at least for high-stakes evidence, to data that carries verifiable provenance from the start.
